title: A training-only false-signal gate beat the response-class rule in seven US air-pollution and wet-deposition families (2005-2024); ozone sensitivity to summer heat fell 39% after 2004
abstract: Question: can training years alone show whether climate terms will add forecast skill in families of abiotic climate-response relations, where a response-class rule says that they will? Approach: we froze the family gate of sci:sha256:6081bf76 (frozen climate slope with a 5-year trailing level if the trend-preserving false-signal rate FSR_T <= 0.32, else a 5-year trailing mean), two nulls and seven predictions in a timestamped plan. We applied them without change to seven US families (3,060 series; training 1980-2004, test 2005-2024): EPA AQS ozone, SO2, NO2, CO and PM10, and NADP wet-deposition ion concentrations and fluxes. Results: the gate closed in all seven families, where the class rule used climate. The gate beat the class rule (pooled skill +0.061, 95% interval 0.049 to 0.076) and chose the better strategy in 6 of 7 families (wet flux was a tie, 0.003). Emission controls moved AQS levels by 2.0-4.5 training standard deviations, and the trailing mean beat the training mean by 85-94%. FSR_T was 1.00 for SO2, NO2 and CO, as predicted. Ozone did not pass the gate (FSR_T 0.61), against our prediction. The detrended slope of annual 4th-highest 8-hour ozone on June-August temperature fell from 4.4 to 2.7 ppb per C (east 5.4 to 2.9; west did not fall; Wilcoxon p = 8e-21). The wet-flux positive control failed: an emission trend hid a real precipitation signal (detrended r 0.52). FSR ordered 25 units of three campaign tests (rho -0.84) but not the seven new families alone. Limitations: one response class and one cause of failure; annual statistics; single linear windows with observed weather; exploratory analyses were defined after the results.
